newsitem.title: UK: Sterling debt and futures closing report.
newsitem.headline: Sterling debt and futures closing report.

text.p: Gilts closed at their session highs on Friday, boosted by buoyant U.S. T-bonds but slightly wary ahead of next week which boasts key U.S. jobs data and the first meeting of Britain's new-style monetary committee.
The June gilt future closed 14/32 higher at 112-20, its high point for the day. Dealers said key resistance just above at 112-21 will be the focal point first thing on Monday.
The contract peaked there on Wednesday before subsiding.

"We've got a big week coming up," said Jonathan York, futures broker at MeesPierson. "The budget date will be announced on Monday, the monetary meeting comes on Thursday and Friday and you've also got non-farm payrolls from the U.S."

A government source told Reuters the date of Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget will be unveiled in a written answer to parliament on Monday. It will probably be held in late June or early July.
But the real action for gilts comes later in the week.
Britain's new monetary set-up, which involves a nine-man committee -- five from the Bank of England and four others chosen by Brown -- meets for two days from Thursday.

Gilt investors will be eager to see who Brown elects to the committee and the identity of the Bank's second deputy governor, yet to be chosen. But it could be the committee has to meet for the first time without a full line-up.

Economists are unsure how likely an immediate rate rise is but Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International, said the Bank's loss of supervisory powers over the City, will increase the pressure to prove its credibility with monetary policy.
"This means there is a greater risk of interest rates heading higher," he said.

David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders added: "There is a good chance that this first meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee will raise rates to 6.5 percent. However, the committee may want to review the contents of Brown's budget speech first."
U.S. non-farm payrolls data, due next Friday, are expected to be firm, up about 250,000 according to Jeremy Hawkins at BankAmerica. That will fuel fears of U.S. interest rate rises.

The United States dominated the gilt market on Friday too. Revised GDP data showed U.S. economic growth up 5.8 percent in the first quarter, the fastest growth rate since late 1987. But economists had been expecting six percent growth, so U.S. Treasuries headed higher, boosting gilts in tandem.
Later data, covering consumer confidence, new home sales and a purchasing managers index on manufacturing all proved softer.

York said gilts were unlikely to outperform much in the days ahead. The gilt/Bund spread stood at 139 basis points late on Friday, in from 142 at Thursday's close. "The spread will continue to hover around 140 for now," he said.
The short sterling strip rallied on Friday with the September contract up three basis points at 93.17 and December gaining four to 93.00. That implies base rates at 6.75 percent by the year-end.

But more importantly in the near-term, the June interest rate contract, which settled at 93.37 on Friday, is just about positioned for a quarter-point increase in 6.25 percent base rates within a month.
